title: Healing and prophecy do not prove a god
source_text: Ἵνα δὲ καὶ δῶ ἰατρόν τινα δαίμονα θεραπεύειν σώματα τὸν καλούμενον Ἀσκληπιὸν, εἴποιμ᾿ ἂν πρὸς τοὺς θαυμάζοντας τὸ τοιοῦτο ἢ τὴν Ἀπόλλωνος μαντείαν ὅτι. εἴπερ μέσον ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν σωμάτων ἰατρικὴ καὶ πρᾶγμα πίπτον οὐκ εἰς ἀστείους μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ φαύλους. μέσον δὲ καὶ ἡ περὶ τῶν μελλόντων πρόγνωσις (οὐ γὰρ πάντως ἐμφαίνει τὸ ἀστεῖον ὁ προγινώσκων), παραστήσατε πῶς οὐδαμῶς μέν εἰσι φαῦλοι οἱ θεραπεύοντες ἢ οἱ προγινώσκοντες παντὶ δὲ τρόπῳ ἀποδείκνυνται ἀστεῖοί τινες καὶ οὐ μακρὰν τοῦ ὑποληφθῆναι εἶναι θεοί. ἀλλ᾿ οὐ δυνήσονται ἀστείους ἀποδεῖξαι τοὺς θεραπεύοντας ἢ τοὺς προγινώσκοντας. πολλῶν καὶ ἀναξίων τοῦ ζῆν θεραπεύεσθαι λεγομένων, οὓς οὐκ ἂν οὐδ᾿ ὁ σοφὸς ἰατρὸς ὢν θεραπεῦσαι ἠθέλησεν ἀκαθηκόντως ζῶντας. καὶ ἐν τοῖς χρησμοῖς δὲ τοῦ Πυθίου εὕροις ἂν προστασσόμενά τινα οὐκ εὔλογα. ὧν δύο ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος παραθήσομαι, ὅτι Κλεομήδην μὲν, οἶμαι τὸν πύκτην, ἰσοθέοις τιμαῖς ἐκέλευε τιμᾶσθαι. οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅ τι ποτὲ σεμνὸν ἰδὼν ἐν τῇ πυκτικῇ αὐτοῦ, οὔτε δὲ Πυθαγόραν οὔτε Σωκράτην ἐτίμησε ταῖς τιμαῖς τοῦ πύκτου. ἀλλὰ καὶ „Μουσῶν θεράποντα“ εἰπὼν τὸν Ἀρχίλοχον. ἄνδρα ἐν κακίστῃ καὶ ἀσελγεστάτῃ ὑποθέσει ἐπιδειξάμενον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ποιητικὴν καὶ ἦθος ἀσελγὲς καὶ ἀκάθαρτον παραστήσαντα. ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ „θεράποντα“ εἶναι „Μουσῶν,“ νομιζομένων εἶναι θεῶν. εὐσεβῆ τινα ἀνηγόρευσεν. οὐκ οἶδα δὲ εἰ καὶ ὁ τυχὼν τὸν εὐσεβῆ φήσει μὴ πάσῃ κεκοσμῆσθαι μετριότητι καὶ ἀρετῇ, καὶ κόσμιος τοιαῦτα λέγοι ἂν, ὁποῖα περιέχουσιν οἱ μὴ σεμνοὶ τοῦ Ἀρχιλόχου ἴαμβοι. εἰ δὲ μηδὲν θεῖον αὐτόθεν ἐμφαίνεται ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀσκληπιοῦ ἰατρικῆς καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος μαντικῆς, πῶς εὐλόγως ἄν τις. ἵνα καὶ δῶ ταῦθ᾿ οὕτως ἔχειν. ὡς θεοὺς αὐτοὺς σέβοι ἂν καθαρούς τινας; καὶ μάλισθ᾿ ὅτε διὰ τοῦ Πυθίου στομίου περικαθεζομένῃ τῇ καλουμένῃ προφήτιδι πνεῦμα διὰ τῶν γυναικείων ὑπεισέρχεται τὸ μαντικὸν, ὁ Ἀπόλλων, τὸ καθαρὸν ἀπὸ γηΐνου σώματος. οὐδὲν δὲ τοιοῦτον ἡμεῖς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ δοξάζομεν. τὸ γὰρ γεγεννημένον ἀπὸ τῆς παρθένου σῶμα ἦν ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ὕλης συνεστηκὸς, δεκτικὸν τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων τραυμάτων καὶ θανάτου.
pass_a_gloss: Even if I grant (δίδωμι, ἵνα καὶ δῶ) that a certain physician demon (ἰατρός δαίμων) heals (θεραπεύω) bodies, the one called Asclepius, I would say to those marvelling (θαυμάζω) at such a thing or at the prophecy (μαντεία) of Apollo that: if the medicine (ἰατρική) of bodies is an indifferent thing (μέσον) and a matter falling (πίπτω) not to the refined/good (ἀστεῖος) only but also to the base (φαῦλος), and foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) of things to come is also indifferent (for the one foreknowing does not wholly display the good, τὸ ἀστεῖον), show (παρίστημι) how those healing or foreknowing are in no way base, but in every way are proved (ἀποδείκνυμι) to be good, and not far from being supposed (ὑπολαμβάνω) to be gods. But they will not be able to prove those healing or foreknowing good, many even unworthy of living (ἀνάξιοι τοῦ ζῆν) being said to be healed, whom not even one being a wise physician (σοφὸς ἰατρός) would have wished to heal, living improperly/against duty (ἀκαθηκόντως). And in the oracles (χρησμοί) of the Pythian (Πύθιος) you would find certain things commanded (προστάσσω) not reasonable (οὐκ εὔλογα); of which I shall set beside (παρατίθημι) two for the present: that Cleomedes, I suppose the boxer (πύκτης), he ordered to be honoured with god-equal honours (ἰσόθεοι τιμαί), I know not what solemn thing (σεμνόν) having seen in his boxing (πυκτική); yet neither Pythagoras nor Socrates did he honour with the honours of the boxer. But also, having called Archilochus 'servant of the Muses' (Μουσῶν θεράπων), a man who displayed his poetic art (ποιητική) on a most evil and most licentious subject (ὑπόθεσις, ἀσελγής) and showed a licentious and impure (ἀκάθαρτος) character (ἦθος), as far as being 'servant of the Muses', reputed to be gods, he proclaimed (ἀναγορεύω) him pious (εὐσεβής). I do not know whether even the chance person (ὁ τυχών) will say that the pious man is not adorned (κοσμέω) with all moderation (μετριότης) and virtue (ἀρετή), and whether an orderly man (κόσμιος) would say such things as the not-solemn iambics (ἴαμβοι) of Archilochus contain. And if nothing divine (θεῖον) is displayed of itself (αὐτόθεν ἐμφαίνεται) from the medicine of Asclepius and the prophecy (μαντική) of Apollo, how reasonably would anyone, even if I grant these things are so, revere (σέβω) them as gods, as certain pure ones (καθαροί)? and especially when through the Pythian opening (στόμιον), to the so-called prophetess (προφῆτις) sitting around it, the prophetic spirit (πνεῦμα μαντικόν), Apollo, the one pure from an earthly body (καθαρὸν ἀπὸ γηΐνου σώματος), steals in (ὑπεισέρχομαι) through the female parts (τὰ γυναικεῖα). But nothing such do we hold (δοξάζω) about Jesus and his power (δύναμις). For the body born (γεννάω) from the virgin (παρθένος) was composed (συνίστημι) of human matter (ἀνθρωπίνη ὕλη), receptive (δεκτικόν) of human wounds (τραύματα) and death.

lemmas.lemma: for the one foreknowing does not wholly display the good, τὸ ἀστεῖον

pass_b_english: Even if I grant that a certain demon who is a physician, the one called Asclepius, heals bodies, I would say to those who marvel at such a thing, or at the prophecy of Apollo: if the healing of bodies is a morally indifferent thing, something that falls to the lot not only of the good but also of the wicked, and if foreknowledge of the future is also indifferent (for the one who foreknows does not necessarily display goodness), then show how those who heal or foreknow are in no way wicked, but are proved by every means to be good, and not far from being thought gods. But they will not be able to prove that those who heal or foreknow are good, since many are said to be healed who are unworthy even to live, whom the wise man, were he a physician, would never have wished to heal, since they live as they ought not.

In the oracles of the Pythian god, too, you would find some commands that are not reasonable. I shall set out two of them for the present. He ordered that Cleomedes, the boxer, I think, be honoured with honours equal to a god's. I do not know what he saw that was so venerable in his boxing; yet he did not honour Pythagoras or Socrates with the honours of the boxer. Again, by calling Archilochus a "servant of the Muses", a man who displayed his poetic art on the vilest and most licentious subject matter and showed a licentious and impure character, he proclaimed him a pious man, in so far as he was a "servant of the Muses", who are reputed to be gods. I do not know whether even an ordinary person would say that the pious man is not adorned with every kind of moderation and virtue, or whether a decent man would say the sort of things contained in the unseemly iambics of Archilochus.

If nothing divine shows itself on its face in the medicine of Asclepius and the prophecy of Apollo, how could anyone reasonably worship them as gods, as pure beings, even if I grant that these things are so? Above all when, through the Pythian vent, the prophetic spirit, Apollo, the one pure of an earthly body, steals into the so-called prophetess through her female parts as she sits over it? We hold no such opinion about Jesus and his power. For the body born of the virgin was made up of human matter, open to human wounds and to death.

choices.choice: μέσον is the Stoic 'indifferent' (neither good nor evil), and ἀστεῖος/φαῦλος are the Stoic pair 'good (worthy)'/'base'; rendered 'morally indifferent', 'good', 'wicked'. ἀκαθηκόντως (contrary to what is fitting, Stoic καθῆκον) rendered 'live as they ought not'. 'οὐκ ἂν οὐδ' ὁ σοφὸς ἰατρὸς ὤν' read with the article on σοφός as the Stoic sage ('the wise man, were he a physician'), in keeping with the Stoic terms around it; the double negative is kept as reinforced negation ('would never'). 'a wise physician' is also possible. Cleomedes is the boxer of Astypalaea whom the Pythia ordered honoured as a hero (story in Pausanias 6.9.6-8; Origen marks the identification with 'I think'); not cited inline. The 'servant of the Muses' oracle about Archilochus is the Delphic response to his killer reported in later writers (e.g. Plutarch); Origen quotes only the phrase, so no inline source. 'οὐκ οἶδα δὲ εἰ καὶ ὁ τυχὼν ... φήσει μὴ ...' kept with its own negation ('would say that the pious man is not adorned'), the sense being that no one would deny it. The last question runs on through 'καὶ μάλισθ' ὅτε', so the Pythia sentence is kept inside the question. 'τὸ καθαρὸν ἀπὸ γηΐνου σώματος' is ironic, applied to Apollo/the spirit. δαίμων rendered 'demon' as elsewhere in this translation. No Scripture quoted; 'born of the virgin' is a statement of doctrine, not a quotation, so no citation.

'since many who are said to be healed are unworthy even of living' -> 'since many are said to be healed who are unworthy even to live' (πολλῶν καὶ ἀναξίων τοῦ ζῆν θεραπεύεσθαι λεγομένων: the unworthy are the subject of 'are said to be healed')
